summary: trench length (L) is what the French drain calculator works out, and it gets there from the trench width, the trench depth, the filter fabric overlap (o) and the trench volume. It suits a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the French drain calculator work?
sections.html:
The French drain calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports trench length (L) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (with fabric filter?, with filter? and the pipe size (Drain pipe details)); then you type in the trench width (w), the trench depth (d), the filter fabric overlap (o) (French drain details) and the trench volume.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the French drain calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Trench length (L)=trench volume ÷ (trench depth (d) × trench width (w))
Volume displaced by drain pipe=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × (outside diameter (Dₒ) ^ 2) × total drain pipe length
Pipe option=(-outside diameter (Dₒ) + outside diameter (Dₒ)) ÷ (outside diameter (Dₒ) − outside diameter (Dₒ))
Trench length (L)=12 × pipe drop ÷ (-pipe option × (outside diameter (Dₒ)) + pipe option × (outside diameter (Dₒ)) + (outside diameter (Dₒ)))
Trench length (L)=the square root of (-(pipe drop ^ 2) + (total drain pipe length ^ 2))
Quantity of pipes needed=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 100) × total drain pipe length ÷ length of available pipes)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The French drain calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the trench width, the trench depth and the filter fabric overlap (o) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the French drain calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns trench length (L), derived from the trench width, the trench depth and the filter fabric overlap (o). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the French drain calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the trench width, the trench depth, the filter fabric overlap (o) and the trench volume, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter trench width (w) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Trench width (w) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (9 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Outside diameter (Dₒ) = 0 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the French drain calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
